title: MCP Apps: Give the Model Data, Give the User a UI — Dustin Mihalik, Indeed
talk_summary: Dustin Mihalik of Indeed describes lessons building MCP apps for Claude/ChatGPT, focused on keeping model-visible data in sync with UI rendering. The core rules: always return structured data alongside any UI, update tool descriptions to tell the model what is displayed, and separate data-processing tools from rendering tools so the model can explore data before choosing what to render.

takeaways.technique: Separate data tools from render tools
takeaways.what_they_do: They split a single 'search jobs' tool that returned UI into a plain text-based search tool the model can call many times, plus a separate render tool that takes a list of IDs the model selected.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to separate your data processing from your UI rendering

takeaways.technique: Return structured data alongside any rendered output
takeaways.what_they_do: Any data shown to a user must also be returned as structured content to the model, kept in sync, otherwise the model is blind to what was displayed and cannot answer follow-ups.
takeaways.evidence_quote: anything that you show to the user also needs to be provided as data to the model

takeaways.technique: Steer model behavior via tool descriptions
takeaways.what_they_do: They edit tool descriptions to state that results are auto-displayed, preventing the model from redundantly re-describing output; a single sentence covered most cases.
takeaways.evidence_quote: results were automatically displayed to the user as UI components at the top of your description

takeaways.technique: Small composable tools over one mega-tool
takeaways.what_they_do: They favor several small tools (multiple search variants, separate render-list vs render-one) with simple descriptions, giving the model flexibility without overloading it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you could build a bunch of much smaller tools. The descriptions can be fairly simple so you don't overload the model
